source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT), v3
finding: GAP 5. The 38.1% UoT headline is a RELATIVE gain, not absolute points. I rebuilt the Llama3-70B figure from Table 1: the mean of per-dataset relative gains over DP, averaged over closed-set and open-set, gives 46.6 exactly.
numbers: Llama3-70B closed-set DP SR 51.4/15.0/83.7/60.2/28.8, UoT 55.9/25.0/90.4/64.3/47.1: mean relative gain 30.8%, absolute +8.7 points. Open-set DP 34.2/15.5/26.0/25.7/11.1, UoT 36.9/21.0/35.6/50.6/26.1: relative 62.5%, absolute +11.5. Average of the two relative gains = 46.6.
quote: UoT enhances the success rate by 38.1% compared to DP across 5 datasets and 5 different LLMs
limits: The paper never says 'relative'; this is inferred by exact arithmetic on one model. Other models were not each rebuilt. Absolute gains are about 9-12 points for Llama3-70B.
agent_relevance: Quote UoT as a relative gain; absolute gains are roughly 9 to 24 points depending on model. Do not plan on 38 points.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT, Table 2 equal-token comparison
finding: GAP 5. At matched tokens (GPT-4, closed set), UoT-style belief plus information-gain search beats self-consistency by a wide margin on 20Q and troubleshooting, and by a smaller margin on diagnosis.
numbers: CoT-SC k=33 (4.6k tokens): 20Q 32.6, MD 37.6, TB 42.5. Pruned UoT D=3 (4.7k tokens): 48.1 / 88.4 / 63.2. Adapted-ToT D=3 (4.5k): 33.8 / 85.1 / 60.3. At about 9k tokens: Adapted-ToT D=4 40.9 / 86.7 / 63.7 vs UoT D=3 54.4 / 92.5 / 66.0.
quote: even when increasing the depth of Adapted ToT (Adapted-ToT (D = 4)) to match the token cost of UoT (D = 3), it still underperforms
limits: Table 2 numbers differ from Table 1 for the same method (CoT-SC 20Q 55.1 in Table 1), so the setting is a different subset. Single run per cell. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: Supports: an explicit hypothesis set plus expected information gain beats sampling many chains at equal tokens. The equal-token part of gap 5 is closed for GPT-4 on these 3 tasks.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT, Appendix H significance
finding: Only three runs per cell were done because of API quota. T-tests still give p<0.05 on all 5 datasets for both GPT-4 and Llama3.
numbers: GPT-4 DP vs UoT: Common 49.0 vs 70.9, Thing 30.8 vs 36.8, DX 89.4 vs 97.0, MedDG 74.9 vs 87.9, FloDial 42.5 vs 67.8. Llama3: 47.7 vs 56.5, 14.8 vs 24.8, 80.1 vs 90.1, 61.3 vs 64.6, 29.9 vs 46.4. Thing (GPT-4) p=0.036 is the weakest.
limits: n=3 runs; a t-test on 3 points is fragile. The answerer is simulated by GPT-4 and was checked on only 10% of dialogues.
agent_relevance: The direction is real; the size is uncertain. The gain is smallest where the base rate is already high (DX 89 to 97).

source: Chattopadhayay and Halder (2026) Belief-State Engine, Tiger main table
finding: GAP 1 and 2. With the exact Bayes posterior and NO decision threshold in the prompt, gpt-4o listened 1.45 times on average before opening a door. The reactive baseline listened zero times. So sensible commit behaviour appeared without a stated stop rule.
numbers: Tiger, T=20, gamma 0.95, N=40 paired seeds, gpt-4o temp 0.3. Success: Reactive 32/40 (80.0%), BSE 38/40 (95.0%), NL-Tracker 32/40. Mean return -12.00 [-25.75, 1.75] vs 3.06 [-4.41, 8.24]. LLM calls per episode 1.00 (reactive) vs 2.45 (BSE).
limits: CIs overlap. N=40, single LLM sampling seed. BSE used 2.45x the LLM calls per episode, so token parity is NOT met. No stated-rule arm exists, so gap 2 (rule vs no rule) is not answered.
agent_relevance: A posterior alone can induce 1-2 evidence-gathering steps. The optimal Tiger rule needs about 2 net hearings, so 1.45 listens is close but not shown optimal.

source: Chattopadhayay and Halder (2026) BSE, what was NOT run
finding: GAP 1. The key comparison is missing. The free-text posterior ablation (AB6) was not run, RockSample was never used, and the NL-Tracker baseline behaved identically to the no-belief Reactive baseline (opens a door on turn 1, zero listens), so it is a weak control.
numbers: Ablations AB3-AB8 and AB10 not executed (text: AB8 and AB10 were not run in this round). Tiger ablation N=25: standard BSE 21/25; AB2 (no observation update): 23/25 episodes time out still listening, mean return -16.08. Decision-consistency probe found zero qualifying history pairs at N=40.
limits: Preprint, two authors, not peer reviewed. The header says April 2026 but the arXiv stamp says September 2026.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays OPEN: no study compares a code-computed posterior with a free-text belief at equal tokens with N>=200.

source: Chattopadhayay and Halder (2026) BSE, attack-graph task
finding: On a larger partially observable task (64 states, 6 nodes) the exact posterior did not separate from baselines on return; only coverage was higher.
numbers: N=40 paired seeds, T=30. Mean return Reactive -5.40 [-17.4, 7.0], BSE -2.80 [-16.0, 10.7], NL-Tracker 7.87 [-5.2, 21.1]. Compromise coverage BSE 42.1% vs Reactive 32.5%.
limits: Point order NL-Tracker > BSE > Reactive is not significant. The patch action was removed from the menu.
agent_relevance: Do not assume an external posterior helps once the state space is big. Evidence so far is one small win and one null.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Bayesian Teaching, Appendix B.2-B.3 verbalised beliefs
finding: GAP 8. For untuned LLMs, stated beliefs and direct actions disagree (under 50% alignment). Making the decision from the stated belief with an external rule was MORE accurate than the LLM's own direct choice. After Bayesian fine-tuning the gap shrinks, except for Qwen 2.5.
numbers: Original LLMs: direct vs belief-derived predictions aligned under 50% (Fig 8c); belief-based accuracy above direct (Fig 8b vs 8a). Humans also showed high inconsistency. Gemma 2 and Llama 3: Bayesian variants had higher consistency than Oracle variants. Qwen 2.5: belief-based accuracy unchanged after tuning.
quote: with less than 50% alignment between the two sets of predictions
limits: Flight recommendation task with simulated users. Values were read from charts and prose, not tables. Belief was elicited in a side branch, not carried in the dialogue.
agent_relevance: Supports forcing the action out of an explicitly stated belief via a code rule: it fixes the mismatch for untuned models. Gap 8 mostly closed for this task.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Self-verification limitations, Table 2
finding: GAP 6. A GPT-4 verifier is wrong in domain-specific ways: the Mystery Blocksworld verifier rejects 97% of correct answers; Graph Colouring rejects 95.8%.
numbers: Game of 24 accuracy 87.0% (3567/4100), FPR 10.4%, FNR 20.7%. Blocksworld 72.4%, FPR 6.5%, FNR 15.48%. Mystery Blocksworld 71.8%, FPR 18.55%, FNR 97.09% (100/103). Graph Colouring FNR 95.8% (113/118).
quote: the verifier requires high accuracy or else the overall system will encounter compounding errors
limits: GPT-4 (2023-era), 100 instances per domain in Table 1. Newer models not tested.
agent_relevance: A weak verifier is worse than none when its false-negative rate is high. Do not discard an answer on an LLM veto alone.

source: Stechly et al. (2024), Table 1 accuracy across schemes
finding: GAP 6. Loss from a weak verifier, measured. LLM self-critique is at or below standard prompting in 3 of 4 domains; a sound verifier gives large gains.
numbers: 100 instances each. Game of 24: standard 5%, LLM+LLM 3%, sound binary feedback 36%. Graph colouring: 16%, 2%, 38%. Blocksworld: 40%, 55%, 60% (binary) up to 87% (all-error feedback). Mystery Blocksworld: 4%, 0%, 10%. Self-consistency k=15: 6%, 14%, 42%, 4%.
limits: Small N. Sound-verifier runs allowed up to 15 rounds, so compute is not matched to standard prompting.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the loss half of gap 6: from +31 points (sound) to -2 points (LLM) on Game of 24.

source: Stechly et al. (2024), appendix A.1 CoT verification
finding: GAP 6. Even a near-perfect LLM verifier is not equal to a sound one, and costs much more.
numbers: Game of 24 verifier accuracy rises from 87% to 99% with chain-of-thought. A 6 percentage point gap to the sound verifier remains in the full pipeline, with 17x output tokens (verification cost more than doubled).
limits: One domain, GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Making an LLM verifier more careful is expensive and still leaks. Prefer programmatic checks (tests, arithmetic, type checks).

source: Lindenbauer et al. (2025) The Complexity Trap: observation masking vs LLM summarization
finding: GAP 4 and 7. On a non-bandit task (SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified, 500 instances, five model setups), hiding old observations matches an LLM summary of history on solve rate and about halves cost versus raw history. Zero-shot, no training.
numbers: Qwen3-Coder 480B solve rate: raw 53.4%, masking 54.8%, LLM-Summary 53.8%; cost about -50% for both. Gemini 2.5 Flash (thinking): masking 36.0% vs summary 35.6%. A hybrid cuts cost a further 7% vs masking and 11% vs summary. Observation tokens are about 84% of a turn.
quote: Observation Masking reduces cost by more than 50% without significantly reducing downstream performance
limits: The row order in the PDF table is garbled for Qwen3-32B, so only unambiguous cells are quoted. One scaffold, one task family. Intervals are +-3 to 4 points, so masking vs summary is within noise.
agent_relevance: For code debugging an LLM summary is not a clear win over dropping stale observations. Prefer cheap deterministic compaction and keep the action history.

source: Lindenbauer et al. (2025), trajectory length effect
finding: GAP 4. LLM summaries made agents run longer, which eats the saving. The authors suggest the summary hides failure signals.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash mean trajectory with LLM-Summary 52 turns: +15% vs masking (44 turns), +4% vs raw (50 turns). Qwen3-Coder 480B: +15% vs raw, +13% vs masking. Summary generation cost up to 7.2% of total instance cost.
quote: context summaries act as a reinforcing signal, encouraging the agent to keep going
limits: The explanation is the authors' hypothesis, not tested by intervention.
agent_relevance: A fluent summary can suppress a stop signal. Link to the commit/stop rule: summaries must keep the failure log, not smooth it.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) PABU: Progress-Aware Belief Update, context ablations
finding: GAP 7. PABU's belief compaction is learned by fine-tuning (Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.1-8B), not prompted. Its own ablation shows which parts of history matter depends on the environment: dropping observation history, action history or available actions each hurts in different tasks.
numbers: Main result 81.0% completion with 9.5 steps (+23.9% relative success, 26.9% fewer steps vs best prior; ATLAS 65.4%, AgentEvol 60.8%). Llama-2-7B-Chat backbone reaches 78.2%.
limits: No zero-shot (prompt-only) PABU arm was found in the text read, so the claim that it helps zero-shot agents is untested there.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 half-closed: zero-shot compaction evidence (d11) shows cost savings with no solve gain; belief-compaction gains come only from trained models.

source: Tang et al. (2026) Tru-POMDP, ablation study
finding: GAP 3. Structure matters more than sample count. Asking the LLM for a flat set of hypotheses in one call was worse than keeping a single best guess. A tree of hypotheses (3 candidates per level) plus Bayesian filtering plus belief tree search was best.
numbers: Branching C1=C2=3 per level. Variants: w/o Belief (single hypothesis), w/o HBU (planning time up to 3x higher), w/o TOH (flat set; worse than single hypothesis), w/o LRP (random rollout, greatly degraded), w/o BTS (lowest reward). Only bar charts with SE; no per-variant numbers in text.
quote: Asking the LLM to generate a flat set of particle hypotheses in a single run degrades belief quality due to hallucination
limits: No sweep over K. Tasks are embodied scene-graph tasks, not reasoning tasks. Figure values not extractable from text.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays OPEN on the best K. Evidence: 3x3 hypotheses work; unstructured many-at-once sampling hurts.

source: Tang et al. (2026) Tru-POMDP, token use and baselines
finding: GAP 3. Tru-POMDP used the fewest LLM tokens among compared planners. LLM-MCTS exceeded the 10-minute limit on every task. ReAct and Reflexion variants reached about 40% success.
numbers: 300 tasks. Figure 3 shows total tokens per episode (read from chart only). LLM-MCTS timed out in all tasks because of repeated LLM calls inside simulation.
limits: An equal-token comparison against one long chain of thought was not run. The baselines are ReAct, Reflexion and LLM-MCTS.
agent_relevance: Particle-style search can be cheaper than naive LLM-in-the-loop MCTS when the rollout policy is written once as code.

source: Somani, Ye, Hsu, Lee (2013) DESPOT: Online POMDP Planning with Regularization, Table 1 note
finding: GAP 9. Implementation variance is real. The DESPOT authors ran the original POMCP code and got worse scores than published, and printed the published numbers beside theirs.
numbers: Table 1 (Tag, LaserTag, RockSample(7,8), (11,11), (15,15), Pocman): POMCP own runs vs published values in parentheses. The PDF table is partly garbled, so only the existence and direction of the gap is firm.
quote: We could not reproduce the earlier published results, possibly because of the code modification and machine differences.
limits: Source read from a local text copy of the paper (title given; the URL is the proceedings index). Exact differences uncertain. No measure of variance across implementations was given.
agent_relevance: Treat planner-vs-planner gaps of a few points as implementation noise unless seeds, code and budget are shared.

source: Henderson et al. (2018) Deep RL that matters, seed variance
finding: GAP 9 (supporting). Same-algorithm runs with different seeds can look significantly different, a larger effect than many reported improvements.
numbers: Two 5-seed sets of the same TRPO configuration gave t=-9.09, p=0.0016 (as already used in K08).
limits: Deep RL on MuJoCo, not LLM agents. Seen this session through the local text copy.
agent_relevance: LLM planner comparisons with N=20 to 40 and one sampling seed (BSE, UoT n=3) cannot resolve differences of a few points.

source: Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis (1987) as restated in Bernstein, Givan, Immerman, Zilberstein (2002)
finding: GAP 10. Confirmed from an opened text that restates the original: the finite-horizon POMDP decision problem is PSPACE-complete and the MDP one is P-complete.
numbers: Text: It was shown in (Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis, 1987) that the decision problem for POMDPs is PSPACE-complete and that the decision problem for MDPs is P-complete.
quote: the decision problem for POMDPs is PSPACE-complete and that the decision problem for MDPs is P-complete
limits: Secondary source. The 1987 paper itself and Puterman's book were still not opened. The PSPACE result is for the finite-horizon decision problem.
agent_relevance: Closes the finite-horizon class question in K02. Justifies bounded search.

source: Madani, Hanks, Condon (1999/2003) Undecidability of probabilistic planning and infinite-horizon POMDPs
finding: GAP 10. Policy existence for infinite-horizon POMDPs is undecidable under discounted, undiscounted total, average reward and state-avoidance models, and this extends to approximation.
numbers: AAAI 1999 abstract opened (truncated). The 2003 journal version (Artificial Intelligence 147) is cited by arXiv 2602.07473 as: no algorithm can compute, or approximate within a non-trivial constant, the maximal reachability probability of a POMDP, while MDP reachability is polynomial-time.
limits: Only the abstract and one 2026 restatement were read, not the proofs. Decidable subclasses exist: posterior-deterministic POMDPs (include all MDPs and Tiger) per 2602.07473.
agent_relevance: Closes the infinite-horizon half of K02. Tiger-like tasks are in a tractable class, so a small hypothesis table is a legitimate exact method there.

source: Chatterjee, Chmelik, Tracol (2013/2016) What is decidable about POMDPs with omega-regular objectives
finding: GAP 10. Quantitative analysis of POMDPs with these objectives is undecidable. Qualitative analysis is undecidable in general but EXPTIME-complete under finite-memory strategies.
numbers: Abstract and introduction opened: EXPTIME-complete qualitative analysis for parity objectives with finite-memory controllers, with optimal exponential memory bounds.
limits: Theory for verification objectives, not reward maximisation.
agent_relevance: Only finite-memory controllers are practically solvable. This matches an agent with a bounded notes table.
